clue.text: Medium-sized milk dish leading couples selected

indicators.note: the leading couple of letters is picked from each word, not the single first letter

parts.note: the leading two letters of MIlk
the leading two letters of DIsh

explanation.surface: A menu description of a middling portion of some milky pudding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Couples' asks for two letters from each word rather than the usual one, so 'leading' here means the first pair.
explanation.definitionFit: Midi is the medium length between mini and maxi, as in a midi skirt.

clue.text: Job needed this report of doctor's clients

indicators.note: a report is something heard, so the answer is what the clients' name sounds like

parts.note: a doctor's clients are patients

explanation.surface: Someone claims Job needed a doctor's report on his clients.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Job' is capitalised because it starts the clue, but it is the Job of the Bible, not employment.
explanation.definitionFit: The patience of Job is proverbial: he endured every trial sent to him.

clue.text: Spoil popular reefs in the middle of the sea

parts.note: to mar is to spoil
in = popular, fashionable

indicators.note: only the central letter of 'reefs' is wanted

parts.note: the middle letter of reEfs

explanation.surface: Tourists are spoiling well-loved reefs out at sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the middle of the sea' reads as one phrase, but it splits: 'in the middle of' works on 'reefs' and 'of the sea' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain adjective synonym: marine life is life of the sea.

clue.text: Hairstyle for every maiden

parts.note: per = for every, as in per head
M is the abbreviation for a maiden over in cricket scoring

explanation.surface: A hairstyle suited to every young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: A maiden in cricket is an over in which no runs are scored, written M on the scorecard.
explanation.definitionFit: A perm is a hairstyle of set waves or curls.

clue.text: Village footpath or pedestrian shelters

indicators.note: the phrase shelters the answer, holding it inside

parts.note: footpaTH OR PEdestrian

explanation.surface: A village scene with a footpath or a pedestrian shelter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shelters' looks like a noun, bus-stop style, but it is a verb: the words before it shelter the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Thorpe is an old word for a village, surviving in English place names like Scunthorpe.

clue.text: Cold-blooded predator caught legendary bird

parts.note: c = caught in cricket scoring
the roc is a giant bird of Arabian legend

explanation.surface: A reptile snaps up a mythical bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Caught' reads as the verb in the surface; it is the scorecard abbreviation C.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal clipping of crocodile, a reptile and so cold-blooded, and a hunter of anything that comes to the water's edge.

clue.text: Capital city the writer's visiting

parts.note: LA = Los Angeles
the writer is the setter, 'I', and 'the writer's' is I'M

explanation.surface: The setter is off visiting a capital city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital city' looks like one unit, but only 'Capital' defines; 'city' is LA.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Peru's capital is one of many capitals.

clue.text: Corporation's software abandoned half written

indicators.note: only half of LEFT is written down

parts.note: an app is a piece of software
abandoned = LEFT, and half of it is LE

explanation.surface: A company has dropped a software project halfway through writing it.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface steers towards software being written; 'abandoned' is LEFT, and 'half written' keeps only its first two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Apple is the corporation behind the iPhone and Mac.

clue.text: Perfect language

definitions.meaning: a verb: to refine something until it is flawless
a noun: the tongue spoken in Warsaw

explanation.walkthrough: The capital P hides the switch: to polish (lower case) is to perfect, and Polish is the language of Poland.
explanation.definitionFit: To polish work is to perfect it; Polish is spoken in Poland.

clue.text: Rosemary sometimes writing "Her Former Majesty" in pencil

indicators.note: writing something in a pencil puts it inside the pencil's letters
'in' says where the letters are written: inside the pencil's two letters

parts.note: HB is the standard pencil grade, hard black
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is how the late Queen signed herself

explanation.surface: Someone called Rosemary sometimes pencils in the words "Her Former Majesty".
explanation.walkthrough: Rosemary looks like a woman's name; it is the herb. 'Sometimes' is there because rosemary is only one example of a herb.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: rosemary is one kitchen plant among many, and 'sometimes' flags that it stands in for the wider class.

clue.text: Cycling with back pulled in likewise revealing gear

indicators.note: the back letter of 'cycling' as BIKING is pulled off
'in' has its back pulled in the same way

parts.note: BIKING without its last letter G
IN without its last letter N

explanation.surface: A cyclist with a stiff back pulls on some rather revealing kit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a preposition joining words together, but it is itself fodder: 'likewise' tells you to cut its back letter just as with BIKING.
explanation.definitionFit: A bikini is a skimpy two-piece swimsuit, revealing gear to wear.

clue.text: "There once was a woman from Tipperary"? Doesn't work in this Irish city
Vacuous criminal makes mad blunders

indicators.note: an empty criminal has lost everything inside, leaving the outer letters

parts.note: CriminaL emptied leaves C and L
to anger someone is to make them mad

explanation.surface: An empty-headed crook makes blunders that drive people mad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vacuous' is a fair description of a criminal in the surface, but here it empties the word of its middle.
explanation.definitionFit: A clanger is British slang for a glaring blunder, as in dropping a clanger.

clue.text: Brought up dirt having swallowed nationalist pride

parts.note: soil = dirt
N = nationalist

explanation.surface: Someone raised in the dirt has swallowed their nationalist pride.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pride' sits at the end as an abstract noun, but it is the collective noun for a group of lions.
explanation.definitionFit: A collective noun: pride is the word for a group of these big cats, so the plural answer fits it.

clue.text: Succeeded picking up inconveniently positioned plant root

parts.note: s = succeeded, in genealogies

indicators.note: picking up a sound is hearing it

parts.note: a weed is a plant growing where it is not wanted

explanation.surface: A gardener managed to pull up an awkwardly placed plant by the root.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'plant root' one phrase; the definition is only 'root', and 'inconveniently positioned plant' is a playful definition of a weed.
explanation.definitionFit: A swede is a root vegetable, called rutabaga in North America.

clue.text: Something additional arising each spring

parts.note: a PS, postscript, is something added to a letter
a = each, as in ten pounds a head

explanation.surface: Something extra turns up every springtime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spring' reads as the season; it is a mineral spring.
explanation.definitionFit: A spa is a mineral spring, or a resort built around one.

clue.text: Turn inside out nevertheless keeping some of the contents

indicators.note: the next word keeps the answer among its contents

parts.note: nEVERTheless

explanation.surface: Emptying a bag inside out, but some of what was in it stays put.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is about a bag's contents; the contents in question are the letters of 'nevertheless'.
explanation.definitionFit: To evert is to turn inside out, a word used of organs in anatomy.

clue.text: Underwear maybe porters put lower for an earl

indicators.note: 'put X for Y' means swap Y out and X in

parts.note: bearers carry loads, as porters do
a lower is something that lows, and an ox lows
EARL with its last letter dropped, a deletion no indicator asks for; the setter appears to have meant 'ear', the part swapped out of BEARERS

explanation.surface: Porters stoop to lay out underwear for an aristocrat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lower' reads as the verb 'to put down', but it is a noun: something that lows, a cow or ox. OX replaces EAR in BEARERS.
explanation.definitionFit: Boxers are loose shorts worn as men's underwear, one kind among many, hence 'maybe'.

clue.text: Setter starts to seem unnecessarily nuanced

indicators.note: the starts of the next three words are taken

parts.note: Seem Unnecessarily Nuanced

explanation.surface: A crossword setter's early clues seem needlessly subtle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Setter' seems to be the compiler, as it so often is; here it is something that sets, the sun.
explanation.definitionFit: The sun sets each evening, so it is a setter.

clue.text: Parade participant heading off someone with a bow

indicators.note: the head, first letter, comes off

parts.note: a MARCHER without its head M

explanation.surface: A marcher peels off from a parade to greet someone with a courtly bow.
explanation.walkthrough: The bow in the surface is a gesture; in the answer it is the weapon.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain description: the bow is the weapon, so the one carrying it to shoot is meant.

clue.text: Act that unites legislative body

definitions.meaning: a formal word for a coming together, including sexual union

explanation.surface: A law that brings together the members of a parliament.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Act' looks like a law passed by the legislature, but it is the act of coming together, including sexual congress.
explanation.definitionFit: The first is a formal word for union, sexual or social; the second is the name of the United States legislature.

clue.text: London borough abolishing old hereditary title

parts.note: a baronetcy is a hereditary title
O = old

explanation.surface: A London council votes to abolish an ancient inherited title.
explanation.walkthrough: BARONET loses its O. A baronet is the lowest hereditary title in Britain, below a baron, addressed as Sir.
explanation.definitionFit: A place defined by its type: an outer borough in north London, whose name is also rhyming slang for hair (Barnet Fair).

clue.text: Oddly identified no address to return automobile

indicators.note: returning sends the letters back the way they came
the odd-numbered letters are the ones identified

parts.note: the 1st, 3rd, 5th, 7th and 9th letters: No Address

explanation.surface: A car with no address has been oddly identified and must go back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Identified' looks like the fodder for 'oddly', but it is part of the instruction; the fodder is 'no address'.
explanation.definitionFit: Sedan is the American word for a saloon car.

clue.text: Hamburger perhaps for one trying to lose weight

definitions.note: an example: someone from Hamburg who might be called Dieter
definitions.meaning: a native of Hamburg, given a typical German first name
an agent noun: a person on a diet

explanation.surface: A hamburger, of all things, for someone on a diet.
explanation.walkthrough: The hamburger is not food but a person from Hamburg, and Dieter is a common German first name.
explanation.definitionFit: The first sense defines by example, a typical German first name for a native of Hamburg; the second is a plain agent noun from 'diet'.

clue.text: Unfortunately omit name for fossil

indicators.note: the letters have come out wrongly arranged

parts.note: anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A regretted omission of a name from a fossil's label.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unfortunately' reads as a comment on the surface but it is the instruction to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: An ammonite is a fossil of a spiral-shelled sea creature.

clue.text: Finished after debut in acting, amateur with lower energy

indicators.note: once past its debut, the word has shed its first letter
the E is moved lower, which in a down answer means further down

parts.note: AMATEUR without its debut letter A

explanation.surface: An amateur actor, once past a first performance, is left with less energy.
explanation.walkthrough: Only one letter moves in the shuffle: E drops two places down the column, so MATEUR becomes MATURE.
explanation.definitionFit: Mature means fully developed, as a finished cheese or wine is.

clue.text: Born in a home sadly ignoring social conventions

parts.note: b = born

indicators.note: the letters have come out badly arranged

parts.note: anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A child born into an unhappy home grows up ignoring social rules.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Born in' looks like one phrase, but 'Born' alone is B and 'in' belongs to the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Bohemian describes an unconventional, artistic way of life.

clue.text: Egg-shaped figure over goal therefore removed

indicators.note: the letters of 'therefore' are removed from the phrase

parts.note: the two words run together
ergo is Latin for therefore

explanation.surface: An egg-shaped figure hangs over the goal and is taken away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over' looks like a positional word telling you where to put something; it is fodder. OVERGOAL loses E, R, G, O in a block.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the word comes from Latin ovum, egg.

clue.text: Limitation of pupil under instruction originally upset teacher

indicators.note: only the original, first letter of 'instruction' is used

parts.note: the first letter of Instruction

indicators.note: in a down answer, upsetting tips the word upside down

parts.note: pupils call a male teacher Sir

explanation.surface: A pupil under instruction is held back, and the teacher is upset.
explanation.walkthrough: Pupil is not a schoolchild but the opening in the eye, which the iris limits.
explanation.definitionFit: The iris sets the size of the pupil, the limit of how much light gets in.

clue.text: As Hegseth would say, bomb West Asian country

definitions.note: the American sense of bomb, a flop
definitions.meaning: Hegseth is a US politician, so this is the American sense of bomb: a failure

explanation.surface: An American defence chief talks of bombing a country in West Asia.
explanation.walkthrough: Pete Hegseth is an American politician, so his 'bomb' is the American sense, a failure; in British English a show that goes a bomb is a hit.
explanation.definitionFit: A turkey is a flop in American slang, and Turkey is a West Asian country.

clue.text: Embodiment of love, painful on the rebound

indicators.note: a rebound comes back, so the word comes back up

parts.note: sore = painful

explanation.surface: Love hurts when you are on the rebound from a break-up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the rebound' is the language of failed romance, and here it just sends SORE backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Eros is the Greek god of love, love personified.

clue.text: Point following better point

indicators.note: 'following' is literal placement: the compass point comes after the word for better

parts.note: to cap a story is to better it
E = east, a point of the compass

explanation.surface: In an argument, one point follows another that tops it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Point' appears twice: the first is a compass point, E, and the last is a headland. 'Better' is a verb, to top.
explanation.definitionFit: A cape is a point of land jutting into the sea.

clue.text: Place in the ground I access after Everton's opener

indicators.note: only the part of ENTER after its opening E is kept

parts.note: I from the clue
access = ENTER, taken after its first letter E, Everton's opener

explanation.surface: A fan gets into the stadium after Everton's first goal.
explanation.walkthrough: Everton is an English Premier League football club from Liverpool, and 'the ground' is its stadium in the surface; Everton's opener is simply its first letter E.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to bury, from Latin in terra, into the earth.

clue.text: Old tax man from Glasgow?

definitions.meaning: a medieval levy, surviving in the phrase for getting off unpunished

definitions.note: an example, hence the question mark
definitions.meaning: a native of Glasgow, standing for his whole nation

explanation.surface: A former taxman who comes from Glasgow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tax man' reads as a tax inspector, but the phrase splits: scot is an old tax, surviving in 'scot-free', and a Glaswegian is a Scot.
explanation.definitionFit: Scot was a medieval tax; a man from Glasgow, Scotland's largest city, is a Scot.
